scenes.animation: A school photo studio: two passport-size prints of Zippy slide out of the printer. Zippy lifts one and drops it exactly on the other; the edges match perfectly and a green 'PERFECT FIT' stamp thumps down.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Neo, these two photos are twins! One sits exactly on top of the other.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In maths, we call them congruent. Same shape and same size.

scenes.animation: Pairs of objects pop up: two identical one-rupee coins, two ice-tray cubes, two equal circles of radius 3 cm. Each pair slides together and overlaps exactly, with the label 'Congruent = equal in all respects'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two figures are congruent if they are of the same shape and the same size.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two circles of the same radius are congruent. Two squares of the same side are congruent.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The test is simple: one covers the other exactly.

scenes.animation: Triangle ABC in blue and triangle PQR in orange. Triangle ABC glides over PQR; as it lands, arrows link A to P, B to Q and C to R. The statement '△ABC ≅ △PQR' writes itself, with the matching letters glowing in the same colours.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two triangles are congruent if the sides and angles of one are equal to the corresponding sides and angles of the other.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Here A falls on P, B on Q and C on R. So we write triangle ABC is congruent to triangle PQR.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Can I also write triangle ABC is congruent to triangle QRP? Same triangle, right?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: No. The order of letters shows which vertex matches which. Writing QRP would pair A with Q, which is wrong.

scenes.animation: A stamp labelled 'CPCT' presses onto the screen and expands to 'Corresponding Parts of Congruent Triangles'. Matching sides of the two triangles flash in pairs: AB with PQ, BC with QR, CA with RP.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Once two triangles are congruent, all their corresponding parts are equal.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: We write this as CPCT, short for corresponding parts of congruent triangles.

scenes.animation: A worked example builds line by line on a chalkboard: 'Given: △ABC ≅ △PQR, AB = 5 cm, BC = 6 cm, ∠B = 40°', then 'A ↔ P, B ↔ Q, C ↔ R', then 'PQ = AB = 5 cm', 'QR = BC = 6 cm', '∠Q = ∠B = 40° (CPCT)'. A yellow 'EXAM TIP' card slides in.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Example: triangle ABC is congruent to triangle PQR. AB is 5 centimetres, BC is 6 centimetres and angle B is 40 degrees.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: First read the correspondence: A matches P, B matches Q, C matches R.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So PQ equals AB, which is 5 centimetres. QR equals BC, which is 6 centimetres. And angle Q equals angle B, which is 40 degrees, by CPCT.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: always write the congruence with vertices in matching order. Examiners check the order.

scenes.animation: Recap board with two overlapping triangles as the icon. Points appear: '1. Congruent = same shape and same size', '2. △ABC ≅ △PQR means A ↔ P, B ↔ Q, C ↔ R', '3. CPCT: corresponding parts are equal'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: congruent figures have the same shape and the same size.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: in a congruence statement, the order of letters tells you which vertex matches which.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: corresponding parts of congruent triangles are equal, or CPCT.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So my photo twins are officially congruent. Framing both!

scenes.animation: Zippy tries to prove two triangles congruent by measuring all six parts with a giant ruler and protractor, getting tangled in measuring tape while a clock spins fast.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Three sides, three angles, two triangles. That's twelve measurements. I'll be here till Diwali!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Relax. You only need three well-chosen parts. Let's meet the shortcuts.

scenes.animation: Two triangles ABC and DEF. Side AB and side DE glow red, the angle at B and the angle at E glow yellow, sides BC and EF glow red. A banner reads 'SAS: Side – included Angle – Side'. The yellow angle sits between the red sides, marked 'included'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The SAS congruence rule: two triangles are congruent if two sides and the included angle of one are equal to two sides and the included angle of the other.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Included means the angle lies between those two sides.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: This rule is taken as an axiom. We accept it without proof.

scenes.animation: A talking protractor named PRO waves a warning flag. It shows two triangles with two equal sides and an equal angle that is NOT between them; they fail to overlap and a red cross appears.

lines.speaker: PRO
lines.text: Careful! If the equal angle is not between the equal sides, the triangles need not be congruent.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So side, side, then some random angle doesn't work?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exactly. The angle must be included.

scenes.animation: Two triangles light up: angle B and angle E in yellow, side BC and side EF in red, angle C and angle F in yellow. Banner 'ASA: Angle – included Side – Angle'. Then a small card flips: 'Two angles known → third angle known (sum = 180°) → AAS works too'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The ASA congruence rule: two triangles are congruent if two angles and the included side of one are equal to two angles and the included side of the other.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Since the angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees, two equal angles make the third angle equal too.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So two angles and any one corresponding side are enough. That is the AAS rule.

scenes.animation: Figure: segments AB and CD cross at O, with A and D on one side. The proof builds line by line: 'OA = OB (given)', 'OD = OC (given)', '∠AOD = ∠BOC (vertically opposite)', '∴ △AOD ≅ △BOC (SAS)', '∠OAD = ∠OBC (CPCT)', 'Alternate angles equal ⇒ AD ∥ BC'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Example: lines AB and CD cross at O, with OA equal to OB and OD equal to OC. Show that triangle AOD is congruent to triangle BOC, and AD is parallel to BC.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: OA equals OB, given. OD equals OC, given. Angle AOD equals angle BOC, because they are vertically opposite.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The angle lies between the two sides, so triangle AOD is congruent to triangle BOC by SAS.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: By CPCT, angle OAD equals angle OBC. These are alternate angles for AD and BC with transversal AB, so AD is parallel to BC.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: write a reason in brackets after every step. Each reason carries marks.

scenes.animation: Recap board with three stickers: '1. SAS: two sides + included angle (axiom)', '2. ASA: two angles + included side', '3. AAS: two angles + any corresponding side'. Zippy rolls up the tangled measuring tape.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: SAS needs two sides and the angle between them.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: ASA needs two angles and the side between them.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: AAS works because the third angle is fixed by the angle sum.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Three parts instead of six. Diwali is saved!

scenes.animation: A samosa on a canteen plate turns into a triangle with two equal sides marked with single ticks. Zippy tilts his head so the samosa looks balanced, like a see-saw.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: This samosa has two equal sides. And it looks perfectly balanced. Coincidence?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Not at all. Equal sides force equal angles. Let's prove it.

scenes.animation: Triangle ABC with AB = AC marked by ticks and the label 'Isosceles'. Then the theorem appears in a box: 'Angles opposite to equal sides of an isosceles triangle are equal', with ∠B and ∠C highlighted.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A triangle with two sides equal is called an isosceles triangle.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Theorem: angles opposite to equal sides of an isosceles triangle are equal.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Here AB equals AC, so we must show angle B equals angle C.

scenes.animation: The proof is built step by step: the bisector AD of ∠A is drawn down to BC, splitting the triangle into △BAD and △CAD. Lines appear: 'AB = AC (given)', '∠BAD = ∠CAD (AD bisects ∠A)', 'AD = AD (common)', '∴ △BAD ≅ △CAD (SAS)', '∴ ∠ABD = ∠ACD (CPCT)', i.e. '∠B = ∠C'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Draw AD, the bisector of angle A, meeting BC at D.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In triangles BAD and CAD: AB equals AC, given. Angle BAD equals angle CAD, since AD bisects angle A. And AD is common.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So triangle BAD is congruent to triangle CAD by SAS.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Therefore angle ABD equals angle ACD by CPCT. That is, angle B equals angle C.

scenes.animation: The theorem box flips over to show its converse: 'Sides opposite to equal angles of a triangle are equal'. Then an equilateral triangle appears, all three sides ticked, and each angle fills with '60°'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The converse is also true: the sides opposite to equal angles of a triangle are equal. It can be proved using ASA.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: What if all three sides are equal?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Then all three angles are equal. They add up to 180 degrees, so each angle of an equilateral triangle is 60 degrees.

scenes.animation: Worked example on a chalkboard, line by line: 'AB = AC, ∠A = 50°', '∠B = ∠C (angles opposite equal sides)', '∠B + ∠C = 180° − 50° = 130°', '∠B = ∠C = 130° ÷ 2 = 65°', 'Check: 50° + 65° + 65° = 180° ✓'. An 'EXAM TIP' card highlights 'opposite'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Example: in triangle ABC, AB equals AC and angle A is 50 degrees. Find angles B and C.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Angle B equals angle C, because they are opposite the equal sides.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Together they make 180 minus 50, which is 130 degrees. So each is 130 divided by 2, which is 65 degrees.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Check: 50 plus 65 plus 65 is 180. Correct.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: the equal angles are opposite the equal sides, not next to the vertex where the equal sides meet.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the balanced samosa icon: '1. Angles opposite equal sides are equal (proof: angle bisector + SAS)', '2. Sides opposite equal angles are equal', '3. Equilateral triangle: each angle = 60°'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: angles opposite to equal sides are equal, proved by drawing the angle bisector and using SAS.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: sides opposite to equal angles are equal.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: each angle of an equilateral triangle is 60 degrees.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Proof complete. Samosa consumed.

scenes.animation: Zippy builds a triangle from three straws joined with thread and tries to squash it into another shape; it refuses to bend. A square of four straws beside it flops into a rhombus instantly.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: My square went floppy, but my triangle won't budge. Is it stubborn?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three fixed sides fix the whole triangle. That idea gives us the SSS rule.

scenes.animation: Two triangles ABC and DEF with all three pairs of sides glowing in matching colours: AB = DE, BC = EF, CA = FD. Banner 'SSS congruence rule'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The SSS congruence rule: if three sides of one triangle are equal to the three sides of another, the two triangles are congruent.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: No angle needs to be measured at all.

scenes.animation: Kite ABCD drawn with AB = AD and CB = CD marked with ticks, diagonal AC in green. Proof lines appear one by one: 'AB = AD (given)', 'CB = CD (given)', 'AC = AC (common)', '∴ △ABC ≅ △ADC (SSS)', '∴ ∠BAC = ∠DAC (CPCT)'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Example: in quadrilateral ABCD, AB equals AD and CB equals CD. Show that AC bisects angle A.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In triangles ABC and ADC: AB equals AD, CB equals CD, and AC is common.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So triangle ABC is congruent to triangle ADC by SSS. By CPCT, angle BAC equals angle DAC. So AC bisects angle A.

scenes.animation: A right triangle with a small square at the right angle; the hypotenuse glows orange. Banner 'RHS: Right angle – Hypotenuse – Side'. A second right triangle slides over it and matches exactly.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The RHS congruence rule is for right triangles.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: If, in two right triangles, the hypotenuse and one side of one triangle are equal to the hypotenuse and one side of the other, the triangles are congruent.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Which side is the hypotenuse again?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The side opposite the right angle. It is always the longest side.

scenes.animation: Triangle ABC with AB = AC and AD ⊥ BC. Proof lines: '∠ADB = ∠ADC = 90°', 'AB = AC (hypotenuse, given)', 'AD = AD (common)', '∴ △ABD ≅ △ACD (RHS)', '∴ BD = CD (CPCT)'. An 'EXAM TIP' card: 'RHS only for right triangles; write R, H and S separately'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Example: in triangle ABC, AB equals AC and AD is perpendicular to BC. Show that D is the mid-point of BC.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Angle ADB and angle ADC are both 90 degrees. Hypotenuse AB equals hypotenuse AC. AD is common.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: So triangle ABD is congruent to triangle ACD by RHS. By CPCT, BD equals CD.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: before using RHS, first state the right angles. Without them, the rule does not apply.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the rigid straw triangle: '1. SSS: three sides equal', '2. RHS: right angle, hypotenuse, one side', '3. Five rules: SAS, ASA, AAS, SSS, RHS'. Zippy stamps 'AAA ✗' with a note 'same shape, different size'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: SSS says three equal sides make two triangles congruent.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: RHS works for right triangles with equal hypotenuses and one equal side.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: our five rules are SAS, ASA, AAS, SSS and RHS. Three equal angles alone are not enough, since the sizes can differ.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: No AAA. Noted, stubborn triangle.
